items.stem: What was the Selma to Montgomery March?
items.stemEs: ¿Qué fue la Marcha de Selma a Montgomery?

choices.text: Four college students sat at a segregated Woolworth lunch counter
choices.textEs: Una marcha de celebración después de que se firmó la Ley de Derechos Civiles

choices.text: A voting rights march where marchers were beaten on Bloody Sunday
choices.textEs: Una marcha por derechos de voto donde marchistas fueron golpeados el Domingo Sangriento

choices.text: Poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and intimidation
choices.textEs: La primera manifestación organizada de derechos civiles en Alabama

choices.text: SCLC protests using children marchers that faced violent response
choices.textEs: Una marcha liderada por estudiantes protestando políticas de segregación escolar

items.explanation: The Selma to Montgomery marches were voting-rights demonstrations in 1965, and the first march became known as Bloody Sunday when troopers attacked protesters on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Choices about bus integration are wrong because Selma focused on the right to vote. The violence helped build support for the Voting Rights Act.
items.explanationEs: The Selma to Montgomery marches were voting-rights demonstrations in 1965, and the first march became known as Bloody Sunday when troopers attacked protesters on the Edmund Pettus Bridge. Choices about bus integración are wrong because Selma focused on the right to vote. The violence helped build support for the derechos de voto Act.

items.stem: The 1960s-70s saw multiple social movements emerge simultaneously: Civil Rights, women's liberation, anti-war, Chicano movement, American Indian Movement, environmental movement, and LGBTQ+ rights. Analyze why so many movements erupted in the same period. Were they separate movements or different expressions of the same underlying forces? Use evidence from at least THREE movements.
items.stemEs: Los 1960-70 vieron emerger múltiples movimientos sociales simultáneamente. Analice por qué tantos movimientos surgieron en el mismo período.
items.correctAnswer: Strong responses should identify common factors (postwar idealism, baby boom demographics, television, Civil Rights Movement as model, disillusionment with Vietnam, expanding higher education) and analyze connections between specific movements while recognizing their distinct identities and sometimes conflicting goals.
items.explanation: A strong response should argue that these movements grew out of shared conditions in the 1960s, including mass media, youth activism, court victories, rising expectations, and frustration with exclusion from power. It should compare at least three movements by showing both overlap and difference, such as civil rights inspiring women's liberation tactics, Chicano activists demanding labor and education reforms, and AIM pressing treaty rights and sovereignty. The strongest essays explain whether these were separate campaigns or linked expressions of a broader struggle for equality, voice, and self-determination.
items.explanationEs: Este ítem DOK 4 requiere analizar la causalidad a nivel social, comparar múltiples movimientos y hacer un argumento sofisticado.

items.stem:
Extended Response — No source is provided for this item. You must draw entirely on your knowledge of U.S. history.

Historians often argue that the Vietnam Era (approximately 1964–1974) represented a turning point in the relationship between the American government and its citizens — one that permanently altered public trust, constitutional norms around war-making, and the willingness of Americans to accept official narratives during times of crisis.

Write an extended response (3–4 paragraphs) in which you:
1. STATE a CLAIM arguing either that the Vietnam Era did or did not represent a permanent turning point in American political culture and constitutional governance.
2. Provide EVIDENCE from at least FOUR of the five standards (US.78–US.82) to support your claim. Your evidence must include specific events, legislation, and the actions of specific individuals or groups — not just general references.
3. REASON through how the evidence you have selected supports your claim, connecting across standards and, where relevant, drawing comparisons to earlier or later periods in American history (e.g., the Civil War era, the Red Scare, the post-9/11 period).

Your argument must be sustained across your entire response and must demonstrate synthesis across the Vietnam Era as a whole — not standard-by-standard description —
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Debes basarte completamente en tu conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU.

Los historiadores a menudo argumentan que la Era de Vietnam (aproximadamente 1964–1974) representó un punto de inflexión en la relación entre el gobierno estadounidense y sus ciudadanos — uno que alteró permanentemente la confianza pública, las normas constitucionales sobre la guerra, y la disposición de los estadounidenses a aceptar narrativas oficiales durante tiempos de crisis.

Escribe una respuesta extendida (3–4 párrafos) en la que:
1. FORMULES un ARGUMENTO argumentando que la Era de Vietnam sí o no representó un punto de inflexión permanente en la cultura política estadounidense y la gobernanza constitucional.
2. Proporciones EVIDENCIA de al menos CUATRO de los cinco estándares (US.78–US.82) para apoyar tu argumento. Tu evidencia debe incluir eventos específicos, legislación y las acciones de individuos o grupos específicos — no solo referencias generales.
3. RAZONAR cómo la evidencia que has seleccionado apoya tu argumento, conectando entre estándares y, cuando sea relevante, estableciendo comparaciones con períodos anteriores o posteriores de la historia estadounidense (p. ej., la era de la Guerra Civil, el Miedo Rojo, el período post-11-S).

Tu argumento debe sostenerse a lo largo de toda tu respuesta y debe demostrar síntesis en toda la Era de Vietnam como un todo — no una descripción estándar por estándar.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4/4) response would include: CLAIM — The Vietnam Era did represent a permanent turning point, not because any single event shattered public trust, but because the convergence of five simultaneous crises — military deception (US.78), mass civic resistance (US.79), constitutional overreach and its rollback (US.80), the expansion of rights movements that challenged government authority on multiple fronts (US.81), and institutional corruption exposed at the highest level (US.82) — together produced structural changes to American governance that have not been reversed. EVIDENCE across standards: US.78 — Gulf of Tonkin Resolution passed on disputed intelligence; Pentagon Papers (1971) proved the Johnson administration deliberately deceived Congress; over 58,000 Americans died; US.79 — the 1969 Moratorium drew ~2 million participants; Kent State killings (May 4, 1970) resulted from the government using military force against its own citizens; VVAW's John Kerry testified before the Senate (April 1971) that veterans had committed war crimes under orders; US.80 — Nixon's secret bombing of Cambodia (Operation Menu, 1969–1970) and invasion of Cambodia (1970) exceeded even the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution's authorization; the War Powers Resolution (1973), passed over Nixon's veto, represented Congress's first statutory limitation on presidential war-making authority since the Constitution; US.81 — Title IX (1972) and the ERA's congressional passage (1972) both reflected demands for federal action that paralleled the anti-war movement's distrust of inherited authority; the women's movement's challenge to institutional sexism mirrored veterans' challenge to institutional militarism; US.82 — Nixon's resignation (August 9, 1974) was the first presidential resignation in U.S. history; the Saturday Night Massacre (October 1973) revealed Nixon's willingness to abuse power; EPA founded 1970 in response to popular environmental mobilization that also reflected distrust of corporate and government authority; the Church Committee (1975) revealed CIA and FBI domestic surveillance programs. REASONING and CROSS-ERA SYNTHESIS — The scale of this transformation becomes clear in comparison: during the Red Scare (1919–1920), government restriction of dissent went largely unchallenged; during McCarthyism (early 1950s), Congress itself participated in civil liberties violations. By contrast, in the Vietnam Era, Congress passed the War Powers Resolution, the Freedom of Information Act amendments (1974), and established the Church Committee to investigate executive branch abuses — representing a structural reassertion of checks and balances unprecedented in the 20th century. The comparison to the post-9/11 period further supports the 'permanent shift' argument: while the Patriot Act (2001) temporarily expanded executive surveillance powers, it triggered immediate legal challenges (ACLU v. NSA) and sunset provisions that reflect the institutionalized skepticism born in the Vietnam Era.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.78, US.79, US.80, US.81, US.82 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: States a defensible, specific claim that takes a clear position on whether the Vietnam Era represented a permanent turning point in political culture and constitutional governance. Draws evidence from at least four of five standards (US.78–US.82), citing specific events, legislation, and named individuals or groups — not general references. Reasoning sustains the argument across all evidence, connecting standards thematically rather than treating them sequentially. Includes at least one meaningful cross-era comparison (e.g., to the Red Scare, the post-9/11 period, or earlier constitutional crises). Writing is sustained, organized, and analytical throughout all 3–4 paragraphs.
3 - Proficient: States a clear claim. Draws evidence from at least three standards with specific events or legislation. Reasoning connects evidence to the claim. May include a cross-era comparison but with limited development. Writing is adequate and organized.
2 - Developing: States a claim but it is vague or inconsistently supported. Evidence drawn from one or two standards, or evidence is general without specific events, legislation, or individuals. Reasoning describes rather than analyzes. No meaningful cross-era synthesis.
1 - Beginning: Restates the prompt or provides a general summary of Vietnam Era events without taking a position or providing sustained analysis. Evidence is absent or purely anecdotal.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964) and disputed intelligence; Pentagon Papers (1971); LBJ and Nixon troop escalation data; Kent State (May 4, 1970); VVAW testimony (1971); War Powers Resolution (1973); Operation Menu (secret Cambodia bombing); Title IX (1972); ERA (1972–1982 ratification timeline); Nixon resignation (August 9, 1974); EPA creation (1970); Church Committee (1975); Freedom of Information Act amendments (1974); Gallup polling data on government trust.
SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: Response should connect across at least four of US.78–US.82 thematically (e.g., the theme of distrust of institutional authority unifying the anti-war movement, the women's movement, the environmental movement, and Watergate); should compare to at least one prior or later historical period; should argue explicitly for or against permanence of the turning point rather than merely describing events.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Formula un argumento defensible y específico que toma una posición clara sobre si la Era de Vietnam representó un punto de inflexión permanente en la cultura política y la gobernanza constitucional. Extrae evidencia de al menos cuatro de los cinco estándares (US.78–US.82), citando eventos específicos, legislación e individuos o grupos nombrados — no referencias generales. El razonamiento sostiene el argumento en toda la evidencia, conectando los estándares temáticamente en lugar de tratarlos secuencialmente. Incluye al menos una comparación entre eras significativa (p. ej., con el Miedo Rojo, el período post-11-S o crisis constitucionales anteriores). La escritura es sostenida, organizada y analítica a lo largo de los 3–4 párrafos.
3 - Competente: Formula un argumento claro. Extrae evidencia de al menos tres estándares con eventos o legislación específicos. El razonamiento conecta la evidencia con el argumento. Puede incluir una comparación entre eras pero con desarrollo limitado. La escritura es adecuada y organizada.
2 - En desarrollo: Formula un argumento pero es vago o inconsistentemente respaldado. Evidencia extraída de uno o dos estándares, o la evidencia es general sin eventos, legislación o individuos específicos. El razonamiento describe en lugar de analizar. Sin síntesis entre eras significativa.
1 - Inicial: Reitera la pregunta o proporciona un resumen general de los eventos de la Era de Vietnam sin tomar posición o proporcionar análisis sostenido.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA: Resolución del Golfo de Tonkín (1964) e inteligencia disputada; Papeles del Pentágono (1971); datos de escalada de tropas de LBJ y Nixon; Kent State (4 de mayo de 1970); testimonio del VVAW (1971); Resolución de Poderes de Guerra (1973); Operación Menú (bombardeo secreto de Camboya); Título IX (1972); ERA (cronología de ratificación 1972–1982); renuncia de Nixon (9 de agosto de 1974); creación de la EPA (1970); Comité Church (1975); enmiendas a la Ley de Libertad de Información (1974); datos de encuestas Gallup sobre confianza gubernamental.
EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: La respuesta debe conectar al menos cuatro de US.78–US.82 temáticamente (p. ej., el tema de la desconfianza en la autoridad institucional que une el movimiento antibelicista, el movimiento de mujeres, el movimiento ambiental y Watergate); debe comparar con al menos un período histórico anterior o posterior; debe argumentar explícitamente a favor o en contra de la permanencia del punto de inflexión en lugar de simplemente describir eventos.

items.stem:
Extended Response — No source is provided for this item. You must draw entirely on your knowledge of U.S. history.

Both the anti-war movement (US.79) and the women's rights movement (US.81) emerged as major forces in American public life during the late 1960s and early 1970s. Historians have debated whether these movements reinforced each other, competed for resources and public attention, or operated largely independently while sharing a common cultural critique of American institutions.

Write an extended response (3–4 paragraphs) in which you:
1. STATE a CLAIM arguing a specific position on the historical relationship between the anti-war movement and the women's rights movement — did they reinforce each other, diverge, or produce a shared transformation of American political culture?
2. Provide EVIDENCE from both US.79 and US.81 to support your claim. Your evidence must include specific organizations, leaders, legislation, events, and dates — not just general descriptions.
3. REASON through how the movements' strategies, goals, and outcomes compare, including where they intersected and where they diverged. Your reasoning should make an argument about the long-term significance of their combined impact, connecting where possible to outcomes after 1974.

Avoid writing a standard-by-standard description. Your argument should be sustained and analytical throughout.
items.stemEs:
Respuesta Extendida — No se proporciona ninguna fuente para este ítem. Debes basarte completamente en tu conocimiento de la historia de EE. UU.

Tanto el movimiento antibelicista (US.79) como el movimiento por los derechos de las mujeres (US.81) surgieron como fuerzas principales en la vida pública estadounidense durante finales de los años 1960 y principios de los 1970. Los historiadores han debatido si estos movimientos se reforzaron mutuamente, compitieron por recursos y atención pública, u operaron en gran medida de forma independiente mientras compartían una crítica cultural común de las instituciones estadounidenses.

Escribe una respuesta extendida (3–4 párrafos) en la que:
1. FORMULES un ARGUMENTO argumentando una posición específica sobre la relación histórica entre el movimiento antibelicista y el movimiento por los derechos de las mujeres — ¿se reforzaron mutuamente, divergieron, o produjeron una transformación compartida de la cultura política estadounidense?
2. Proporciones EVIDENCIA de US.79 y US.81 para apoyar tu argumento. Tu evidencia debe incluir organizaciones específicas, líderes, legislación, eventos y fechas — no solo descripciones generales.
3. RAZONAR cómo se comparan las estrategias, los objetivos y los resultados de los movimientos, incluyendo dónde se intersectaron y dónde divergieron. Tu razonamiento debe formular un argumento sobre la importancia a largo plazo de su impacto combinado, conectando donde sea posible con resultados después de 1974.

Evita escribir una descripción estándar por estándar. Tu argumento debe ser sostenido y analítico a lo largo de toda tu respuesta.
items.correctAnswer: A top-score (4/4) response would include: CLAIM — The anti-war movement and the women's rights movement of the late 1960s and early 1970s reinforced each other in their shared critique of institutional authority and their common use of mass mobilization, consciousness-raising, and legislative pressure — yet they diverged significantly in their legal strategies and long-term outcomes, with women's rights producing more durable legislative change while the anti-war movement's influence depended on the specific crisis of Vietnam. EVIDENCE from US.79: Students for a Democratic Society (SDS) and the Port Huron Statement (1962) articulating participatory democracy; the 1969 Moratorium to End the War (~2 million participants); Kent State killings (May 4, 1970) following Nixon's Cambodia invasion; Vietnam Veterans Against the War (VVAW) and John Kerry's Senate testimony (April 22, 1971); the draft lottery (1969) as a galvanizing factor for young men; the publication of the Pentagon Papers (June 1971) and the New York Times v. United States Supreme Court decision (1971); the 26th Amendment (1971) lowering the voting age to 18 in direct response to the argument that those old enough to fight should be old enough to vote. EVIDENCE from US.81: Betty Friedan's founding of NOW (1966) and publication of The Feminine Mystique (1963); Shirley Chisholm's 1972 presidential campaign; the ERA's congressional passage (1972) and Phyllis Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign; Title IX of the Education Amendments (1972); the Senate hearings on women's rights (1970, used as public domain substitute for private feminist writings); Roe v. Wade (1973) expanding reproductive rights; the ACLU Women's Rights Project and Ruth Bader Ginsburg's systematic litigation strategy; women's athletic participation growing from ~294,000 to over 2 million after Title IX. REASONING — The movements intersected most clearly in their shared challenge to institutional legitimacy: anti-war protesters challenged military authority; feminists challenged domestic, educational, and professional authority. Both used mass demonstrations, congressional testimony, and Supreme Court litigation. They diverged in durability: the anti-war movement dissolved after the Paris Peace Accords (1973) and U.S. withdrawal, while the women's rights movement institutionalized its gains through Title IX enforcement, expanded litigation, and ongoing legislative advocacy. The 26th Amendment (US.79) and Title IX (US.81) both illustrate how social movements translated protest into lasting constitutional or statutory change — the most significant long-term legacy of the era's activism.
items.dokRationale: Student must synthesize across multiple standards and sources, constructing an extended argument that connects US.79, US.81 through evidence-based reasoning requiring sustained analytical writing.
items.explanation:
SCORING GUIDE (4 points):
4 - Exemplary: States a defensible, specific claim that takes a clear position on the relationship between the anti-war and women's rights movements — reinforcing, diverging, or transforming political culture together. Draws specific evidence from both US.79 and US.81, naming specific organizations, leaders, legislation, events, and dates. Reasoning sustains the argument by comparing and contrasting the movements' strategies, goals, and outcomes, and makes an explicit argument about long-term significance. Writing is analytical, organized, and sustained throughout all 3–4 paragraphs. Avoids standard-by-standard structure.
3 - Proficient: States a clear claim about the relationship between the two movements. Draws specific evidence from both US.79 and US.81. Reasoning compares the movements' strategies or outcomes. May not fully develop the long-term significance argument. Writing is adequate and organized.
2 - Developing: States a claim but treats the two movements separately rather than in relationship to each other. Evidence is present but general (mentions 'anti-war protests' or 'women's rights' without specific organizations, events, or dates). Reasoning describes rather than analyzes the relationship. Little to no cross-movement synthesis.
1 - Beginning: Provides a general description of one or both movements without taking a position on their relationship. No sustained claim. Evidence is absent or anecdotal. No synthesis.
0 - No response or completely off-topic.

KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED (US.79): SDS and Port Huron Statement (1962); 1969 Moratorium (~2 million); Kent State (May 4, 1970); VVAW and Kerry testimony (April 1971); draft lottery (1969); Pentagon Papers (1971); 26th Amendment (1971).
KEY EVIDENCE EXPECTED (US.81): NOW founded 1966 (Betty Friedan); Shirley Chisholm 1972 presidential campaign; ERA passed Congress 1972, Schlafly's Stop ERA campaign; Title IX (1972); Roe v. Wade (1973); RBG/ACLU Women's Rights Project; women's athletic participation data post-Title IX.
SYNTHESIS EXPECTATIONS: Response should compare strategies (demonstration, legislation, litigation) across both movements; should identify at least one explicit intersection (e.g., 26th Amendment argument connecting military service to voting rights; women in anti-war organizations); should make an argument about which movement's gains proved more durable and why; should connect to outcomes after 1974.
items.explanationEs:
GUÍA DE PUNTUACIÓN (4 puntos):
4 - Ejemplar: Formula un argumento defensible y específico que toma una posición clara sobre la relación entre los movimientos antibelicista y de derechos de las mujeres — reforzándose, divergiendo o transformando juntos la cultura política. Extrae evidencia específica de US.79 y US.81, nombrando organizaciones, líderes, legislación, eventos y fechas específicos. El razonamiento sostiene el argumento comparando y contrastando las estrategias, los objetivos y los resultados de los movimientos, y formula un argumento explícito sobre su importancia a largo plazo. La escritura es analítica, organizada y sostenida a lo largo de los 3–4 párrafos. Evita la estructura estándar por estándar.
3 - Competente: Formula un argumento claro sobre la relación entre los dos movimientos. Extrae evidencia específica de US.79 y US.81. El razonamiento compara las estrategias o resultados de los movimientos. Puede no desarrollar completamente el argumento de significado a largo plazo. La escritura es adecuada y organizada.
2 - En desarrollo: Formula un argumento pero trata los dos movimientos por separado en lugar de en relación entre sí. La evidencia está presente pero es general. El razonamiento describe en lugar de analizar la relación. Poca o ninguna síntesis entre movimientos.
1 - Inicial: Proporciona una descripción general de uno o ambos movimientos sin tomar posición sobre su relación. Sin argumento sostenido. Sin síntesis.
0 - Sin respuesta o completamente fuera del tema.

EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA (US.79): SDS y Declaración de Port Huron (1962); Moratoria de 1969 (~2 millones); Kent State (4 de mayo de 1970); VVAW y testimonio de Kerry (abril 1971); lotería de reclutamiento (1969); Papeles del Pentágono (1971); 26.ª Enmienda (1971).
EVIDENCIA CLAVE ESPERADA (US.81): NOW fundada en 1966 (Betty Friedan); campaña presidencial de Shirley Chisholm en 1972; ERA aprobada por el Congreso en 1972, campaña Stop ERA de Schlafly; Título IX (1972); Roe v. Wade (1973); Proyecto de Derechos de la Mujer de RBG/ACLU; datos de participación atlética femenina post-Título IX.
EXPECTATIVAS DE SÍNTESIS: La respuesta debe comparar estrategias (manifestación, legislación, litigación) en ambos movimientos; debe identificar al menos una intersección explícita (p. ej., el argumento de la 26.ª Enmienda que conecta el servicio militar con el derecho al voto; mujeres en organizaciones antibelicistas); debe formular un argumento sobre qué conquistas del movimiento resultaron más duraderas y por qué; debe conectar con resultados después de 1974.
